title: Ami Bera Wins Eighth Term, Extends Record as Longest-Serving Indian American Lawmaker
excerpt: The California Democrat defeated Republican Robb Tucker in the redrawn 3rd district and returns to senior roles on foreign affairs and intelligence.
body:
• Ami Bera, 61, has won an eighth term in the US House of Representatives, defeating Republican Robb Tucker in California's 3rd congressional district.
  • Bera is the longest-serving Indian American in Congress, having represented Sacramento County since 2013; he ran in the 3rd district this year after California's redistricting.
  • He returns as ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific and as a member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
  • Bera has been a prominent voice on US-India ties, criticising the $100,000 H-1B visa fee and the 50 per cent tariff on India.

Ami Bera, the son of Indian immigrants and the longest-serving Indian American now in Congress, has won an eighth term in the US House of Representatives. Bera defeated Republican Robb Tucker in California's 3rd congressional district, IANS reported on November 4.

Bera, 61, has represented Sacramento County since 2013. He ran this year in the 3rd district after California's redistricting. With the victory, the physician-turned-politician Amerish Babulal 'Ami' Bera extends a congressional career that began when he was first elected in 2012 and took office in January 2013. Coverage of the result is available from IANS and Connected to India.

A senior voice on foreign affairs

Bera returns to Washington as a senior Democrat on foreign affairs and intelligence. He is the ranking member of the Foreign Affairs Committee's subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific and sits on the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. He is a member of the New Democrat Coalition, and his official website lists health care availability and affordability, the Sacramento region and national security as his focus.

In 2015, Bera became co-chair of the Congressional Caucus on India and Indian Americans, the first Indian American to hold the post. He is among the House members who mark Diwali on Capitol Hill.

India, H-1B and tariffs

Bera's new term begins at a time of strain in ties between Washington and New Delhi. He led a five-member congressional delegation to India in September 2025, just as the Trump administration announced a $100,000 fee on H-1B visas.

"If President Trump were to ask me what to do, I'd say pick up the phone and call Prime Minister Modi."

— Ami Bera, on US tariffs on India

On the H-1B fee, Bera said at the time that it was a poorly thought through policy, that much lower fees of $1,000 to $4,000 were more appropriate, and that the fee could push tech companies to expand in Hyderabad or Bangalore instead of creating American jobs. At a December 2025 congressional hearing, he said the fee disadvantages US companies. After an additional 25 per cent tariff on India over its purchases of Russian oil brought the total to 50 per cent, Bera urged direct diplomacy and said a 50 per cent tariff on a good friend was not where policy should go.

Background and campaign

Bera was born in Los Angeles in 1965 to Gujarati immigrant parents who emigrated from Rajkot in Gujarat. He attended public schools through medical school and earned his undergraduate and medical degrees at the University of California, Irvine, graduating with less than $10,000 in debt, according to his website. He practised medicine for 20 years, served as chief medical officer for Sacramento County, and later as a clinical professor at the UC Davis School of Medicine.

IANS described Bera as the most centrist of the three Indian American Democrats re-elected on Tuesday, citing Voteview DW-NOMINATE scores that rank him 190th most liberal among House Democrats. His campaign raised about $1.5 million in the 2026 cycle and had about $1.7 million in cash on hand as of October 14, according to Federal Election Commission filings cited by IANS.

For Indian American voters, Bera's return preserves the community's most senior voice in the House on the issues that most directly link the diaspora to India: work visas, trade and the bilateral relationship itself.
